parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian айва́ (ajvá).

Borrowed from Ukrainian баво́вна (bavóvna), itself a mistranslation of Russian хлопо́к (xlopók, “crack, snap, pop”), a euphemism for an explosion, as хло́пок (xlópok, “cotton”) by automated translation tools.
Borrowed from Ukrainian банду́ра (bandúra).
From ба́тя (bátja) + -ко (-ko); originally a diminutive. Cognates include Ukrainian ба́тько (bátʹko), Belarusian ба́цька (bácʹka). This spelling is probably influenced by Ukrainian.

Borrowed from Ukrainian бідолага (bidolaha, “poor thing, poor person”), from an earlier бідолаха related to Ukrainian біда (bida), which is a cognate with Russian беда (beda). The word has been adapted to the Russian phonetics with the change of "і" in Ukrainian біда (bida) to "е" like in Russian бе

From бу́да (búda) + -ка (-ka), the former of which has been displaced by the suffixed formation and is from Ukrainian бу́да (búda), from Polish buda, from Middle High German buode = German Bude, from Proto-Germanic *bōdō as English booth.
Borrowed from Ukrainian бу́льба (búlʹba) and Belarusian бу́льба (búlʹba).

parole.significato: vatrushka (a sort of small, round cottage cheese-filled pastry)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian ватру́шка (vatrúška).

parole.significato: "viy" (a creature with gigantic eyelids and eyelashes from hell who kills by looking at people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian вій (vij).
Borrowed from Ukrainian вишива́нка (vyšyvánka).

parole.significato: a Ukrainian ultranationalist; especially one who is seen to behave like a vatnik.
parole.testo: From вышива́нка (vyšivánka, “Ukrainian traditional clothing”) and ва́тник (vátnik, “quilted jacket, Russian ultranationalist”), in turn derived from Ukrainian вишива́нка (vyšyvánka). Coined in response to the vatnik memes mocking Russian nationalists.
Borrowed from Ukrainian гай (haj), from Proto-Slavic *gajь. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian гај/gaj, Slovene gaj, Slovak háj.

parole.significato: a kind of dumpling with no filling, normally added to soups, halušky
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian галу́шка (halúška), from Polish gałuszka, from gałka (“ball, knob; jaw; testicles”), gały (“eyes”). Compare Russian га́лка (gálka, “glass ball”), Belarusian га́лы (hály, “eyes, buttocks”), Slovene gȃłka (“oak gall, nutgall”) (tonal orthography), Slovak hálka (“ball; top of a

Borrowed from Ukrainian гноби́ти (hnobýty), from Proto-Slavic *gnobiti. According to Pokorny, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gnet-; compare Proto-Slavic *gnesti (“to press”), Proto-Germanic *knudaną.

parole.significato: a famine with mass deaths, especially one of the Soviet famines in 1921–22, 1932–33, or 1946–47
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian голодомо́р (holodomór). Compare го́лод (gólod, “hunger”) and мор (mor, “plague, pestilence”), мори́ть (morítʹ, “to kill, to exterminate”).

parole.significato: vodka, usually in a Ukrainian context.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian горі́лка (horílka). Akin to горе́ть (gorétʹ, “to burn”), Ukrainian горі́ти (horíty, “to burn”). Similar to Belarusian гарэ́лка (harélka). Note гора́льник (gorálʹnik) (< гора́ть (gorátʹ), a causative of горе́ть (gorétʹ)) (compare typologically виноку́р (vinokúr) <+ кури́ть (ku
From Ukrainian дба́ти (dbáty) and/or Belarusian дбаць (dbacʹ), from Old Ruthenian дба́ти (dbáti), possibly from Old Polish dbać, from Proto-Slavic *dъbati. Cognate with Polish dbać, Czech dbát.
Adaptation of Ukrainian двобій (dvobij) which, along with many other cognates, is eventually descended from Proto-Slavic *dъva (“two”) + *bojь (“fight”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian дівча́та (divčáta), the plural of Ukrainian дівча́ (divčá).

Borrowed from Ukrainian дітвора (ditvora) during XIX century, which was derived from Old East Slavic дѣтъва (dětŭva) (compare derivation of мошкара (moškara)), from Proto-Slavic *dětъva. Compare Polish dziatwa.

parole.significato: girl (usually in the Ukrainian or dialectal (Kuban or Don river) contexts)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian ді́вчина (dívčyna) or дівчи́на (divčýna).

parole.significato: didukh (a Ukrainian decoration made from sheaves of wheat tied up with colorful ribbons, which is used in rituals aroun…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian діду́х (didúx), from дід (did, “grandfather”) + -ух (-ux, augmentative suffix).

parole.significato: fool, idiot, imbecile (person with poor judgement or little intelligence)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian ду́рень (dúrenʹ). By surface analysis, дурно́й (durnój) + -ень (-enʹ).

parole.significato: the palm with the fingers bent so that they could scoop up, grab or hold something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian жме́ня (žménja). Compare typologically гра́бка (grábka) (usually гра́бки pl (grábki), akin to гра́бить (grábitʹ), грести́ (grestí), граба́стать (grabástatʹ), also note гра́бли pl (grábli), загребу́щий (zagrebúščij)),

parole.significato: yellow and blue (the colors of the Ukrainian flag)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian жо́вто-блаки́тний (žóvto-blakýtnyj, “yellow-blue”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian заробітчанин (zarobitčanyn), from Ukrainian заробіток (zarobitok, “wages”), which is cognate with за́работок (zárabotok).

parole.significato: katsap, a Russian person, Russian, Russki
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian каца́п (kacáp).
Borrowed from Ukrainian квито́к (kvytók), derived from Polish kwit.

parole.significato: kobza (old Ukrainian music instrument, a kind of lute)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian ко́бза (kóbza), from Proto-Turkic *kopuŕ via a Turkic language.
Borrowed from Ukrainian кобза́р (kobzár), influenced by -арь (-arʹ)
First attested in c. 2022, but in common usage only as of 2023. Borrowed from Ukrainian контрна́ступ (kontrnástup).

parole.significato: a type of large, unleavened flatbread
parole.testo: First attested in the 19th century, borrowed from Ukrainian корж (korž).

parole.significato: a Zaporozhian Cossack village or township
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian курі́нь (kurínʹ), from Turkic. Attested at least since 1572.
Borrowed from Ukrainian курку́ль (kurkúlʹ).
Via Ukrainian лати́нь (latýnʹ) from Old East Slavic латинъ (latinŭ), from Latin latinus.

Borrowed from Ukrainian люби́сток (ljubýstok), from Polish lubszczek (modern lubczyk), from Middle High German lübestecke (> German Liebstöckel), from Latin levisticum, earlier ligusticum, from Ancient Greek λιγυστικόν (ligustikón), originally “Ligurian plant used for medicinal purposes”.

parole.significato: doll, puppet (a toy in the form of a human)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian ля́лька (ljálʹka), from Polish lalka.
From Ukrainian and Belarusian мо́ва (móva). Doublet of молва́ (molvá).

parole.significato: a Ukrainian-speaker who hates the Russian language
parole.testo: From мо́ва (móva, “[Ukrainian] language”) + говню́к (govnjúk, “shit-eater”), ultimately from Ukrainian мова (mova, “language”)
Corruption of мо́ва (móva), making it similar to etymology 1 above, from Ukrainian and Belarusian мо́ва (móva, “language”).

parole.significato: independent (used in a satirical and derogatory context in relation to Ukraine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian незале́жний (nezaléžnyj).

Borrowed from Ukrainian нікче́мний (nikčémnyj) in late 19th or early 20th century, from Old Ruthenian никче́мный (nikčémnyj), possibly from Old Polish nikczemny. By surface analysis, ни (ni) + к (k) + чему́ (čemú) + -ный (-nyj).

Borrowed from Ukrainian нудни́й (nudnýj), from Old Ruthenian нꙋдны́й (nudnýj, “boring”), from Old East Slavic нꙋдьнъ (nudĭnŭ, “gruelling, difficult”), from Proto-Slavic *nudьnъ. By surface analysis, ну́да (núda) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: to seize, to grip, to overcome, to overwhelm (especially of feelings)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian обу́рювати (obúrjuvaty) of broader meaning “to irritate, to make irate, to revolt or shock, to enrage”, perfective обу́рити (obúryty), from о- (o-) + бу́рити (búryty, “to stir, to shake; to flurry, to trouble”).

parole.significato: glaze, glaze ice, glazed frost, verglas, sleet
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian о́желедь (óželedʹ), from Proto-Slavic *o(b)želdь, from Proto-Slavic *o(b)- + *želdь.
Borrowed from Ukrainian очиток (očytok), from очисник (očysnyk, “cleaner”). Further from чи́стий (čýstyj, “clean”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian па́рубок (párubok). See also ребёнок (rebjónok).
Borrowed from Ukrainian пацю́к (pacjúk). Cognates include Belarusian пацу́к (pacúk).

parole.significato: boy, kid, lad, fella (referring to a boy or a young man; can be used as a term of address)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian пацан (pacan) during Soviet era, see more there.

parole.significato: field pea (Pisum sativum subsp. arvense syn. Pisum sativum convar. speciosum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian пелю́шка (peljúška).

parole.significato: victory, triumph (especially of Armed Forces of Ukraine, or of anything Ukrainian in general, often implying the opposi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian перемо́га (peremóha), analysable as a deverbal from перемо́чь (peremóčʹ) but the borrowing is recent.
Borrowed from Ukrainian перемо́га (peremóha), mocking the pronunciation of "г" as a "h" (which the closest equivalent in Russian is х (x)).
Borrowed from Ukrainian повста́нець (povstánecʹ)

parole.significato: pole (either of the two points on the earth's surface around which it rotates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian по́люс (póljus), from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos).

Borrowed from Ukrainian рагу́ль (rahúlʹ), used since the 1960's among Russians in Lviv, and spread all over western Ukraine. Various etymologies suggest that this term was originally from рог (rog, “a horn”) or рога́тка (rogátka, “a slingshot, a turnpike”). The latter referred to barriers that kept
Borrowed from Ukrainian рушни́к (rušnýk). Doublet of ручни́к (ručník).

parole.significato: politically conscious (used in a satirical context in relation to Ukrainian nationalists)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian свідомий (svidomyj, “aware, conscious”), from Polish świadomy. It may also be influenced by the word содо́мия (sodómija, “sodomy, homosexuality, perversion”). Compare the semantic development of English woke.
Borrowed from Ukrainian склеп (sklep, “vault, crypt”), borrowed from Polish sklep (“vault, cellar, crypt”), from Proto-Slavic *sъklepъ. Doublet of склёп (skljop), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: а mixture of wheat and rye, barley and rye, barley and oats, and similar; maslin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian су́ржик (súržyk).
Borrowed from Ukrainian си́рник (sýrnyk). By surface analysis, сыр (syr) + -ник (-nik), though сыр (syr) is not usually used to refer to quark in Russian.
Borrowed from Ukrainian так са́мо (tak sámo).
Borrowed from Ukrainian тіка́ти (tikáty).
Borrowed from Ukrainian тмин (tmyn), кмин (kmyn), тмін (tmin), кмін (kmin), from Polish kmin, via Middle High German from Latin cumīnum.

Borrowed from Ukrainian тапчан (tapčan), from Crimean Tatar [Term?], from Middle Chinese 道場 probably via Mongolian, a calque of Sanskrit बोधिमण्ड (bodhimaṇḍa). Compare Ukrainian тапчан (tapčan), Polish tapczan and Kazakh тапшан.

parole.significato: trembita (an alpine horn made of wood)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian трембіта (trembita), from Hungarian trombita, from Italian trombetta, diminutive of tromba.
Borrowed from Ukrainian ха́та (xáta, “house; home”), from Proto-Slavic *xata, from Scythian.
Borrowed from Ukrainian хло́пець (xlópecʹ, “boy, lad”), cognate to Polish chłopiec.
Borrowed from Ukrainian ху́стка (xústka) or Belarusian ху́стка (xústka), cf. Polish chustka.
Borrowed from Ukrainian ціка́вий (cikávyj)
From Ukrainian цу́цик (cúcyk), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *cucьkъ (“dog, puppy”).

Borrowed from Ukrainian череви́к (čerevýk), from Old East Slavic черевикъ (čerevikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *červikъ (“shoe”), from *červo (whence Russian чре́во (črévo, “belly, womb, inside, interior”)). Doublet of череви́цы (čerevícy), inherited directly from East Slavic.
Borrowed from Ukrainian шаровари (šarovary) no later than the 16th century, from Turkish şalvar, from Persian شلوار (šalvâr).
Borrowed from Ukrainian шкі́рка (škírka, “diminutive of шкі́ра (škíra)”). Cognate with Russian шку́ра (škúra, “skin”) (from Polish).
Borrowed from Ukrainian шлях (šljax) or Belarusian шлях (šljax), cf. Polish szlach or szlak.
Distorted form of что (što), possibly influenced by Ukrainian що (ščo).
